description: Turkic Islamic empire (1299–1922) that dominated the Middle East, North Africa, southeastern Europe, and the Caucasus for six centuries; Mehmed II's conquest of Constantinople (1453) ended Byzantine continuity and positioned the Ottomans as the successor empire of Rome; their administrative devşirme system, legal innovations, and religious tolerance of dhimmi communities created the most durable Islamic imperial structure in history.

lifecycle_phases.description: Mehmed II's conquest of Constantinople (1453) ends the Byzantine Empire and gives the Ottomans control of the Bosphorus. He reorganizes the empire on a systematic basis: the devshirme system provides Janissaries, the timar system organizes provincial cavalry, and the millet system governs non-Muslim communities. Selim I (1512–1520) defeats the Safavids at Chaldiran (1514) and conquers the Mamluk Sultanate (1517), making the Ottomans guardians of Mecca and Medina.

Suleiman I 'the Magnificent' represents the peak of Ottoman power. He captures Belgrade (1521), destroys the Kingdom of Hungary at Mohács (1526), and besieges Vienna (1529). The Ottoman navy under Barbarossa dominates the Mediterranean. Suleiman's legal codifications earn him the title 'Lawgiver' in the Islamic world. The empire stretches from Algeria to Mesopotamia, and Hungary to Yemen.

After Constantinople's fall, the empire systematically eliminates the remaining Christian states of the Balkans: Serbia (1459), the Byzantine successor states (Trebizond 1461), Bosnia (1463), and Wallachia becomes a vassal. Venice cedes Cyprus (1573 in later period). The empire reaches peak territorial expansion that defines the medieval-to-early modern transition.

rise_factors.description: Ottoman use of large-caliber siege artillery, including the massive bombards that breached Constantinople's walls in 1453, gave them decisive advantage over any fortification in Europe or the Near East; their combined-arms system (artillery, Janissaries, sipahi cavalry) was the most sophisticated in the world

The devshirme-timar-millet system created a uniquely efficient imperial administration: Christian slave-soldiers loyal only to the sultan, provincial cavalry paid in land grants rather than cash, and autonomous religious communities managing their own civil affairs, minimizing resistance while maximizing military output

Control of Constantinople gave the Ottomans command of the only sea passage between the Black Sea and Mediterranean; this chokepoint made the empire the mandatory intermediary for Black Sea trade and gave it leverage over Genoese and Venetian commercial networks

The janissary corps, slave soldiers recruited via the devshirme system from Christian populations, created a professional standing army loyal to the sultan rather than to competing Muslim noble families. This gave Ottoman sultans coercive capacity unavailable to rivals.

The millet system granted non-Muslim communities (Orthodox Christians, Jews, Armenians) legal autonomy over personal status law. This pragmatic tolerance enabled Ottoman rule over enormously diverse populations without the cost of forced conversion.

Mehmed II's capture of Constantinople (1453), using cannon to breach Theodosian walls that had held for 1,000 years, ended Byzantine civilization and gave the Ottomans the most psychologically significant capital in the medieval world.

Ottoman control of Anatolia's productive agricultural land, combined with the timar system that assigned land revenues to military service, created a sustainable fiscal-military system that Roman-Byzantine-style pay armies had never achieved.

decline_factors.description: Ottoman succession was decided by fratricide, the first act of a new sultan was typically to execute all male relatives; while brutal, this eliminated competitors, but the system created court factions around princes and harem politics that destabilized governance

By Suleiman's death (1566), the empire stretched across three continents; simultaneous military pressure from the Habsburgs in the west, the Safavids in the east, and the Portuguese in the Indian Ocean exceeded the administrative and logistical capacity of even the Ottoman system

Ottoman law effectively required new sultans to execute all brothers to prevent succession wars. While stabilizing individual successions, this practice repeatedly eliminated competent military and administrative talent, and created psychological pressure on the institution.
